children.text: A small island in Romblon just over
1 hour
by boat from Boracay, known locally as Hambil. With its less-developed white sand beaches, cliff-diving spots, and cave exploration, it's popular with travelers looking to escape Boracay's crowds.

Administratively, Carabao Island belongs to Romblon province, but geographically it's a small island right next to Caticlan at the northern tip of Panay and just north of Boracay. The whole island is a single municipality called San Jose, and locals call it 'Hambil' after its old name. It's close enough that on a clear day you can see the island's ridgeline over the horizon from Boracay's Station 1 beach.

The island covers about 22 km² and, according to the 2024 census, has about 11,600 residents. It is divided into five barangays: Busay, Combot, Lanas, Pinamihagan, and Poblacion (formerly called Agogon). Indigenous people of Aeta descent live alongside settlers who came over from Panay. The main language is Onhan, the same one spoken around Aklan. During the Spanish period the island was called Hambil, and it is said to have been named Carabao because its shape resembles a water buffalo; San Jose became an independent municipality on
July 1, 1968
. Fishing and tourism are the residents' main sources of income.

What draws attention to this island is an atmosphere that recalls 'Boracay 20 to 30 years ago.' It has fine white sand similar to Boracay's, but no large resorts, malls, or all-night parties. Most islanders work in fishing and farming; bangkas line the beach, and in the evening children swim in the sea. With fewer tourist facilities there are inconveniences too, but that simplicity is exactly the appeal.

The terrain is characterized by limestone cliffs, so caves and rock ledges are common along the coast. This has made Carabao Island known as a cliff-diving spot in the western Visayas, and you can also swim into sea caves. The beaches on the island's west and south sides are good spots to see the sunset together with a view of Boracay.

It suits travelers who want to rest somewhere quiet for a day or two during a Boracay trip, young travelers who love adventurous water play, and those who want a close look at everyday life in a Philippine island village. On the other hand, travelers who want convenient facilities and a variety of restaurants would be better off with just a day trip.

The island's most famous cliff-diving spot, with rock ledges of varying heights to jump from into the sea. It also has an underwater cave passage, making it popular with confident swimmers, and the entrance fee is about
A coastal cave with an interior space as tall as a cathedral ceiling, with a diving platform set up inside for jumping into the sea. It's safer to enter with a local guide.

blocks.title: Lanas Beach and San Jose Beach

children.text: Lanas Beach in the west is an endless stretch of fine white sand with lovely views at sunset, while San Jose Beach in the east, next to the Poblacion port, is a palm-lined beach good for watching the sunrise. Lanas is about
15 minutes
from the port by motorcycle. Either way, there are few people, so it feels as if you have the whole beach to yourself.
A hilltop viewpoint in the island's interior and a sunset spot with a sweeping view of Boracay, Caticlan, and the Aklan coast. You have to go up by motorcycle, the entrance fee is about
, and it's best to arrive
30 minutes
before sunset.

Hire a motorcycle taxi for half a day and tour the beaches, caves, and viewpoints all at once. The driver, who knows the island's road conditions and the locations of its sights, effectively acts as a guide.
A cave once home to countless bats, where you can see the island's limestone terrain up close. The interior is dark and slippery, so bring a flashlight and sturdy shoes.
Hire a bangka and go snorkeling around the island's coral areas and small beaches. With fewer boats than Boracay, many spots have relatively healthy coral.

The fare for a chartered bangka is set in advance and includes the round trip and waiting time. If you also want to see the sunset at Tagaytay Point, the return trip will be in the dark, so it's safer to stay overnight on the island.

From Manila to Caticlan Airport (MPH) takes about
1 hour
, and about
1 hour 5 minutes
to Kalibo Airport (KLO). Caticlan Airport is much more convenient since it's close to the port; if you land at Kalibo, you'll need another
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by van to Caticlan. There are also direct flights to Caticlan and Kalibo from Cebu.
There are also direct flights to Caticlan from Clark Airport, about two to three a day, taking about
1 hour 15 minutes
, which is convenient when departing from north of Manila or Angeles.
Caticlan Airport's runway is
long and handles aircraft up to the A321 class. From Manila, Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and Philippines AirAsia operate direct flights, and promo fares start from around
one way. Construction of a new passenger terminal began on

The island has almost no taxis or jeepneys; habal-habal (motorcycle taxis) are the main mode of transport. A half-day to full-day charter to tour the sights is negotiated at around
per person. There are also a few tricycles.
Scooter rental is about
a day (it varies by shop and by transmission type), and a motorcycle taxi from the port to Lanas is negotiated at around

The dry season from
November
to
May
is best.
January–April
especially has calm seas and clear skies, suited to bangka travel and cliff diving.
March–May
is very hot, but the water color is at its most beautiful.
From
June
to
October

is the rainy season, and the southwest monsoon roughens the sea on the island's west side. During this period, the small bangkas linking Caticlan and the island are often canceled, and the Philippine Coast Guard sometimes suspends small-boat operations. Typhoons mostly pass through this area in
July–November
, so build extra time into your schedule. Pairing your trip with nearby Kalibo's Ati-Atihan Festival (the third week of
January
) also lets you enjoy Panay's festival atmosphere.
Temperatures in the dry season are generally around
. In
December–January
the northeast monsoon makes the sea calmest, and
March–May
is the hottest. The peak seasons are
December–February
and the
March–April
holidays, when accommodations fill up early. Typhoons have halted boats recently, too. When Typhoon Opong passed Romblon in
September 2025
, passenger ferry service was suspended, and during Super Typhoon Indey in
July 2026
, several routes around Romblon and Caticlan were also canceled.

Accommodations are scattered around Poblacion (the area around San Jose port) and Lanas Beach. Local guesthouses cost about
per night, and beachfront bungalows and small resorts run about
. There are a few mid-range resorts with swimming pools, but there are few of them, so book ahead in peak season (
December–May
) and on holidays. Most accommodations either provide meals or let you use the kitchen.
A well-known place is Lanas Beach Resort, right on Lanas Beach. It's a small beach resort with nine rooms, starting from around
per night, with its own restaurant and good sunsets. Ocean's Edge Resort on the Poblacion side has about 50 rooms, a swimming pool, and a private beach, at about
per night, one of the higher price ranges on the island. The Beach House is a mid-range property with a private beach and snorkeling close by. They are small, so book ahead for
December–May

Food on the island is simple. Tinola (chicken soup), kinilaw (a raw fish salad), and charcoal-grilled fish are common, and some places will cook fish you bought at the market in your accommodation's kitchen for a small cooking fee. You can also try tuba, a traditional drink made from coconut sap, in the villages. Accommodation restaurants sometimes require advance orders, so ask about dinner time when you arrive.

There aren't many restaurants on the island, so most travelers rely on their accommodation's restaurant and local carinderias (small eateries). Grilled fish caught that day, squid, shellfish dishes, and kinilaw are common, and in the morning you can buy fresh fish at the market near the port and ask your accommodation to cook it. There are no convenience stores or large supermarkets, so buy snacks, bottled water, and your favorite drinks in Caticlan beforehand.
There are no ATMs on the island. Withdraw enough cash in Caticlan or Boracay to cover accommodation, transport, and entrance fees.
Mobile signal is generally available, but weak in the island's interior and near the caves. Accommodation Wi-Fi can also be slow.
Public boats leaving the island often depart at dawn, so it's safer to be back in Caticlan or Boracay the day before your return flight.
Before cliff diving, always check the water depth and safe entry points with a local guide, and start from the lower spots first.
Aqua shoes and a waterproof bag are essential. The caves and rocky shoreline are slippery and sharp.
Before boarding a habal-habal, clearly agree on the route, total fare, and waiting time.
In Caticlan, you need to go to the jetty where Carabao Island bangkas dock, not the jetty port for Boracay. Tell your tricycle driver clearly that you're headed 'to Hambil' or 'to San Jose.'

Boat ticket fares bought in Caticlan often include the environmental fee, so keep your receipt or boarding pass. Entrance fees for the caves, cliffs, and viewpoints are paid in cash on site, so have plenty of small bills of
, and
ready.
Watch the sunrise at San Jose Beach in the east, and the sunset at Lanas Beach in the west or at Tagaytay Point. To see both in one day, rent or charter a motorcycle to get around.
The risk of a cliff jump varies with water depth and the tide. At Cathedral Cave the lower side is about
and the higher side about
, at Koding-Koding Point it's about
, and at Busay about
, so start from the lower spots at first.
Cliff diving carries a high risk of injury. Never jump after drinking, and wear a life vest if you're not a confident swimmer.
Small bangkas rock heavily in high waves. Wear a life vest, and don't insist on departing when weather conditions are bad.
There's no large hospital on the island, so emergencies require transport to Caticlan or Kalibo. Be sure to bring a basic medical kit.
Don't leave trash on the beaches or in the caves, and don't damage the coral or cave life.
Roads are dark at night, so avoid riding a motorcycle late in the evening.

Cave diving and cave swimming can run into a blocked entrance or stronger currents when the waves are high or the tide is in. On days when the sea is rough, do not enter, even if a local guide tries to talk you out of it.
Boat services can be canceled without notice depending on the weather. Always build in about a day of buffer time for this island.
